sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Clark County, Ohio?
sections.html:
The Clark County Recorder works from the A.B. Graham Building at 31 North Limestone Street, Springfield, OH 45502. The county's staff directory gives 937-521-1705 for the office and 937-328-4620 for its fax line.

The same building holds the county auditor and the treasurer, which helps a seller in Springfield who has to visit more than one counter. The county's public records page links a Recorder's Office Title Search and a Land Records and Property Alerts page, so you can look up a recorded deed or a lien before you list or sign.

Springfield is the county seat. Owners in New Carlisle, in the townships or in the villages file at the same Limestone Street office, since one recorder serves the whole county.

sections.h2: What do recording fees look like in Clark County?
sections.html:
The amounts come from section 317.32 of the Revised Code, which every Ohio recorder follows. Each charge is a base fee plus a housing trust fund fee of equal size, and a county may add a document preservation surcharge of up to $5 per instrument. Ask the Clark County office which surcharge amount it applies, and request its current sheet, because the statute says "up to" and has been amended several times.

Recorder fees set by Ohio Revised Code 317.32, base fee plus housing trust fund fee

Photocopy at the counter, per page$1$1

Pages are measured at 8.5 by 14 inches, and the caption page counts. A deed of three pages therefore costs more than a deed of two.

sections.h2: What does the Clark County auditor handle before a deed is recorded?
sections.html:
In Ohio the deed goes to the county auditor before it reaches the recorder. Section 319.202 has the grantee or the grantee's representative file a statement declaring the property's value, either electronically or as three paper copies. The auditor then endorses the deed to show the fee charged. The Clark County Auditor's office is at 31 N. Limestone Street, and its printed phone number is 937-521-1860.

Three charges can be involved, and the Clark County Auditor can tell you which apply:

  • The auditor's statement fee under section 319.54(G)(3): $1, or ten cents for each $100 or fraction of $100, whichever is greater.
  • A county real property transfer tax, which section 322.02 lets commissioners levy at no more than thirty cents per $100 after two public hearings. Whether Clark County levies it is a question for the auditor.
  • The recorder's own charges from the table above.

The grantor pays the auditor's fee and any transfer tax. The seller's closing statement should show them as a line item.

sections.h2: What must the seller tell the buyer about tax reductions?
sections.html:
Section 319.202 ties the deed to the property tax bill. The buyer's statement must either affirm that the seller was asked whether the current or preceding year's taxes will be cut under section 323.152 and answered no, or come with a sworn instrument that estimates the reduction. Those reductions include the homestead credit and the owner-occupancy credit.

A second question covers current agricultural use valuation. If the land was enrolled in that program, the statement must say that a recoupment charge may follow when the land stops qualifying. Clark County has farmland outside Springfield, so a seller of a rural parcel should ask the auditor about enrollment before signing the deed.

sections.h2: Which Clark County transfers carry no auditor fee?
sections.html:
Section 319.54(G)(3) exempts some transfers from the statement fee. The exempt reason must be written on the statement. The grounds a Clark County seller may meet include:

  • A transfer to or from the United States, Ohio or an agency or political subdivision of either.
  • A sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A deed that gives or releases security for a debt.
  • A transfer where the value does not exceed $100.
  • A conveyance with no money or other valuable consideration, as long as it is not a gift.
  • A lease, unless the term is renewable forever.

The statute has more categories than these. When a deed falls under one, the auditor's office provides the exemption form to use in place of the value statement.

sections.h2: How do you check Clark County records and guard against deed fraud?
sections.html:
The county's public records page points to the recorder's title search tool and to a land records site that offers property alerts. A property alert watches a name or parcel and notifies you when something new is filed against it. Owners of rental houses, inherited houses and vacant houses benefit most, because a forged deed is easiest to slip through when nobody is living in the home.

Before closing, a title company searches the same records for liens, unreleased mortgages and judgments. If a mortgage was paid off years ago but no release was ever recorded, the release has to be filed before a clean title can pass, and the recorder charges per instrument for it.

sections.h2: What is Clark County like for a house seller?
sections.html:
Clark County lies in west central Ohio and covers 403 square miles, which makes it the third smallest county in the state by total area. It was created on March 1, 1818 and named for George Rogers Clark. Springfield and New Carlisle are its two cities, and Champaign, Madison, Greene, Montgomery and Miami counties border it. Springfield sits on the Mad River, Buck Creek and Beaver Creek, about 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton, and Wittenberg University and Clark State College are based there.

  • Population: 135,340 in July 2025, which is 0.5 percent below the April 2020 base.
  • Housing units: 61,550 in July 2025.
  • Owner-occupied rate, 2020 to 2024: 69.4 percent.
  • Median value of owner-occupied units, 2020 to 2024: $169,900.
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $872.

These are Census QuickFacts numbers for the county as a whole. Springfield residents are mostly in the Springfield City School District, with parts of the north in Northeastern Local and Northwestern Local and parts of the west and south in Clark-Shawnee Local, according to the city's Wikipedia entry.

sections.h2: How should a Clark County owner handle recording in a fast sale?
sections.html:
A cash sale still passes through the auditor and then the recorder, and a title company or closing attorney usually carries the papers. If the house came through an estate, confirm that the person signing the deed has authority from the probate court first. Paying a lien or a back tax bill before closing keeps the recording step simple.

Ask three things before the signing date: whether the county levies a transfer tax, what the recorder charges for the page count of your deed, and whether any old mortgage still lacks a recorded release.

faqs.q: Where is the Clark County recorder's office?
faqs.a: It is in the A.B. Graham Building at 31 North Limestone Street in Springfield, OH 45502. The county directory lists the office phone as 937-521-1705.

faqs.q: How much does the first page of a deed cost in Clark County?
faqs.a: Ohio law sets the first two pages at a $17 base fee plus a $17 housing trust fund fee, and a county may add a surcharge of up to $5. Ask the Clark County recorder what surcharge applies and what the current sheet shows.

faqs.q: Does Clark County charge a real property transfer tax?
faqs.a: Ohio lets a county levy one at up to thirty cents per $100 of value, but the county auditor is the office that knows whether Clark County does. Ask before closing, because the grantor pays it with the auditor's fee.

faqs.q: Can I search Clark County deeds online?
faqs.a: Yes. The county's public records page links a Recorder's Office Title Search and a Land Records and Property Alerts page. Use the alerts to be told when a document is filed against your name or parcel.

faqs.q: Do I record the deed first or go to the auditor first?
faqs.a: Go to the auditor first. Under section 319.202 the grantee's statement of value is filed with the auditor, who endorses the deed. The endorsed deed then goes to the recorder.
